input.title: The Beacons of Caphereus
input.world_description:
Troy is ash. Ten years of siege have collapsed into a single week of fire, and the harbour below the broken walls has become the last patch of Achaean ground on Asian soil. It is a temporary city of hulls and mud: black ships drawn up in ranks along the shingle, rope and pitch and looted bronze stacked in the tide line, cook-fires burning where women who were queens yesterday now sit bound and silent. Everyone here is waiting on the wind, and the wind, all agree, has not been asked for properly.

Two names hang over this harbour, though only one man answers to his. **Telamonian Ajax**, the Bulwark, second only to Achilles in the ten years of fighting, is not among the living. He took his own life on the Trojan plain after the armor of the dead Achilles was awarded to Odysseus rather than to him, and his barrow stands apart at **Rhoeteum**, a headland north of the main camp, raised in haste and already treated as holy ground. Oarsmen touch the hilt of a blade before rowing past it. The Salaminian contingent, his own men, camp nearest the mound under his half-brother **Teucer**, and they have not forgiven the army for the verdict that killed him; they load their ships slowly, and they watch the Atreidae with the particular patience of men counting a debt.

The living Ajax is **Oilean Ajax**, called the Locrian, small and quick and the fastest runner at Troy after Achilles, commander of the Locrian spearmen. In the chaos of the sack he dragged the Trojan priestess **Cassandra** from the altar of Athena's temple within the citadel, and in doing so tore her hands from the goddess's cult image. The army knows this happened. Most of the army has decided not to know it. **Agamemnon**, who wants Cassandra for himself as a war-prize, has quietly refused to let the priests bring the matter to trial, and this refusal is the second debt now accumulating in the harbour, alongside the first. Athena, patroness of the citadel that was violated, is owed a reckoning that no one present is willing to pay.

The harbour itself is a place of factions rather than unity. The **Salaminians** under Teucer, grieving and half-estranged from the high command. The **Locrians**, proud of their small fast ships and increasingly isolated as rumor of the temple spreads crew to crew. The household of **Agamemnon and Menelaus**, the Atreidae, who hold the authority to order the fleet out but not, everyone suspects, the favor of the gods to see it home. The seer **Calchas**, who read the omens that started this war at Aulis and is asked now, again, to read the omens that might end it safely, and who this time says nothing, which frightens the captains more than a bad prophecy would. And offshore, unseen but spoken of at every fire, **Nauplius**, king of Euboea, whose son Palamedes was stoned to death on a false charge of treason engineered by Odysseus years ago, and who has waited a decade for the Achaean fleet to sail past his coast so that he might collect on that grief.

The geography of the voyage is already infamous before a single ship has left the beach. The fleet must round **Euboea**, and specifically the strait of the **Euripus**, whose tides are said to reverse themselves seven or eight times a day for no reason any sailor has ever explained, swallowing ships that misjudge the turn. Beyond it lie the **Gyrean rocks**, a jagged reef with no safe channel through, and beyond that the cliffs of **Cape Caphereus**, sheer, current-scoured, and lightless except for whatever fires a man chooses to build on them. Nauplius is known to keep watch-fires on high ground along this coast, ostensibly beacons of welcome. Every captain in the harbour has heard the story of a false beacon lit on a false headland to draw a grieving father's enemies onto the rocks, and every captain intends to trust his own pilot over any light he cannot vouch for, and every captain knows that intention and practice diverge in a storm.

Overhead, the omens are bad and getting worse. Sacrificial smoke bends wrong. Birds that should fly out to sea circle back over the tents. A priestess of Athena, one of the few still willing to speak plainly, has said openly on the beach that the goddess wants either the guilty man surrendered and stoned, or a fleet that sails without her blessing and takes its chances with Poseidon's water and its own pride. Nobody has surrendered anybody. The ships are being loaded anyway.

So the harbour holds its breath between two unresolved debts, owed to two different powers, both incurred by conduct toward or judgment concerning an Ajax, and both due for payment somewhere on the black water between Troy and home. What sails out of this harbour, and by what course, and under what captain's stubbornness or caution, will decide how much of the Achaean fleet ever sees Mycenae, Salamis, or Locris again. The tomb at Rhoeteum will still be there when the ships return, if they return; the question the world poses is what will be left to come back to it.
